newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal January inflation boosts market optimism.
newsitem.headline: Portugal January inflation boosts market optimism.

text.p: Portugal's consumer prices rose less than predicted in January, strengthening confidence in the government's 1997 goal of getting inflation down below the limit for entry to monetary union.

The National Statistics Institute (INE) reported that the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.3 percent month-on-month in January, against a 0.1 percent rise in December, while the year-on-year rate was unchanged at 3.3 percent.
But analysts had feared that the month-on-month rate could go as high as 0.8 percent in January when the government adjusts centrally-administered prices such as public transport and telephones.

"The CPI (in January) showed that there are no inflationary tensions in the economy and, in the coming months, the year-on-year rate is going to fall slightly," said analyst Martin Amaral Neto of Banco ESSI.

The government forecasts that inflation, as measured by a rolling 12-month average, will fall to 2.25-2.50 percent by the end of the year from 3.2 percent in January. A rate of 2.5 percent should be good enough for entry to Economic and Monetaryion (EMU), government officials say.

According to a Finance Ministry study, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, the average rate will peak at 3.3 percent in March before beginning a slow decline to reach the 2.5 percent in December.

"It was a very promising start to the year," said economist Isabel Cabral of brokers Fincor about the January figures. "By the end of the year, I continue to believe that an average rate of 2.5 percent is achievable."

Analysts said that they expected a sharp reduction in the year-on-year rate around the middle of the year, with the figure possibly even dropping below two percent, as the impact on prices of last year's mad cow disease scare works its way out of the system.
"We think that in May, the CPI (year-on-year) could break two percent and go to 1.9 percent," said analyst Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
But some analysts warned that it was important to know the pace of non-tradable goods prices, basically wages, before coming to clear conclusions on the inflation trend.
Non-tradable goods prices rose 4.9 percent in December but no breakdown has been issued yet for January.

"We still need to know about non-tradable goods. Tradable goods prices are in line with the rest of Europe but it is the non-tradable that is important," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist at Banco Portugues de Investimento.
Nevertheless, analysts said that they did not expect the Bank of Portugal to cut interest rates on Tuesday when it announced conditions for the next commercial bank reserve period.
The main reason why the Bank was expected to be cautious was the recent volatility on the foreign exchange market where the escudo, along with the Spanish peseta, has lost ground on the German mark.
